U.S. ordering some government staff to depart Saudi Arabia, reducing military footprint in Middle East
By Olivia Gazis and Joe Walsh — Updated on: October 21, 2026 / 7:28 PM EDT / CBS News

The U.S. State Department has ordered non-essential U.S. embassy personnel to depart Saudi Arabia, following an uptick in attacks on the kingdom by Iran-backed Houthi militants.

The U.S. military has also been quietly reducing its footprint at posts in the Middle East due to ongoing regional threats from the Houthis and direct threats from Iran, a U.S. official and a senior U.S. military official told CBS News on Wednesday.

State Department spokesperson Tommy Pigott stated: "issued an ordered departure for non-emergency U.S. government employees and their family members in Saudi Arabia only," pushing back on a report that orders could apply to other Gulf states.

CBS News has learned several other embassies adjusted their staffing under "restricted operations" status, but have not gone on ordered departure, which involves the mandatory evacuation of designated diplomatic staff and accompanying family due to security risks.

The decision to draw down personnel in Saudi Arabia comes after U.S. embassies issued warnings over the weekend, urging Americans in the region to exercise caution and prepare for travel disruptions due to Houthi attacks.

Pigott said: "Iranian-supported Houthis have increasingly engaged in hostilities against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian airports and other critical infrastructure resulting in civilian casualties and severe travel disruptions."

The Houthis have launched drones and missiles at airports and oil facilities in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, including a strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport earlier this month that killed 12 people and injured more than 300 others. One American was among those killed.

Ambassador Marwan Ali Noman, political adviser to the Foreign Minister of Yemen, stated: "We are fighting on behalf of everyone, because the threat and risk of the Houthis will expand," adding that the Yemeni government is seeking international assistance.

President Trump did not rule out strikes on the Houthis after the group's deadly October 10 attack on the Riyadh airport, telling reporters: "We may."

Mr. Trump said: "We have communication with the Houthis, and we'll see what happens. But what they did was very bad."
